1:
Seven days of silence end here, and the voices set the scene before weighing the speech. Clarke has the three friends awed and confounded at an unprecedented affliction, until Eliphaz, having heard the complaint, forgets that he came as a comforter and not a reprover, and loses the feeling of the friend in the haughtiness of the censor. Gill supposes more deliberation, a consultation in which the three settled a plan and the order of proceeding, and notes that Eliphaz was probably the senior of them, which is why he begins and why the Lord at the end addresses him by name. Ellicott, who thinks awe should have kept Eliphaz silent, states the premise that governs everything the friends will say: that it is the wicked who suffer, and that all who suffer must therefore be wicked. In one form or another, he observes, that is the sum and substance of their whole case.

The opening itself is read as unusually careful. Henry notes the modesty of a man who will not undertake the cause alone but joins his friends to it, and who promises only to assay something pertinent, as many excellent discourses have gone under the modest title of essays; Wesley says the same in fewer words. Henry also hears real tenderness in the question whether a word will grieve him, and draws the rule that we ought to be afraid of grieving any, especially those already in grief. Against that he sets the counterweight, that it is foolish pity not to reprove a friend in affliction merely for fear of giving offence.

The first charge is faint-heartedness, and Henry grants that there was too much ground for it. He dwells first on what Eliphaz concedes, that Job had instructed many, not thinking it beneath him, with a dexterity in fortifying people against temptation that strengthened weak hands and feeble knees. Why Eliphaz should recall it Henry reads two ways, either as a preface meant to make the reproof passable, or as an aggravation that turns the physician's own medicine against him. Clarke puts the second more bluntly: either Job pretended to what he did not have, or he is failing to use the principles he recommended to others. Henry then catches something the others miss. Eliphaz says only that the trouble touches Job, which is the very word Satan had used twice; had Eliphaz felt half the affliction he would have said it smote or wounded him. And on the other side of the same verse he finds the resentment overstated, since men in deep distress must have grains of allowance, and when we make the worst of every word we do not as we would be done by.

The second charge, that the piety was never real, Henry calls utterly groundless and unjust, and identifies with Satan's own aim, since those who pass rash and uncharitable censures on their brethren serve his interest more than they know. A character, Henry adds, is not to be taken from a single act. On what moved Eliphaz the voices then divide. Clarke, who had called him a censor, still judges the beginning plausible and far from insincere, since it is a duty to rise up on God's part even at the cost of grieving a friend. Ellicott finds instead a conspicuous want of feeling, allowing that the outward signs of sympathy were given, and thinks Eliphaz almost rejoices that one who had helped so many now needs help himself. The verse that closes the charge is itself unsettled. Ellicott offers two senses, one asking whether Job's piety should not have been his confidence, the other whether it is not shown worthless by his fainting, and judges the drift the same either way; Clarke thinks an older English version hit it by asking where Job's fear of God, his patience and the perfectness of his life are now.
7:
Eliphaz now asks whether anyone innocent ever perished, and the voices divide over its force and its truth. Wesley takes it as the accusation it sounds like, that Job must be guilty of some secret crime which has now found him out. Ellicott offers a gentler account of the object, which he thinks more probable and certainly more gracious: not that Job is sinful, but that if he is what he was taken to be, this is itself a ground of hope, since no innocent person is allowed to perish. He calls it a half-truth that is after all true, since God will never fail, though he may try, those who trust him. Henry will not let it stand. If the perishing meant is final and eternal, the principle holds but is misapplied, since a man is never undone till he is in hell; if it means temporal calamity, it is simply false, and instances enough existed before Job's own time to contradict it. Was not Abel innocent, and cut off in the beginning of his days? Was not Lot burnt out of house and harbour? Gill sifts the words to the same end, since no man is free of sin and the righteous plainly do die, so that the claim can only concern a violent death.

The proverb about ploughing iniquity and reaping the same is the part every voice is comfortable with. Clarke gathers the parallels, from Solomon on sowing iniquity and reaping vanity to the prophet's sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind, which he notes uses almost the same words as Eliphaz, and adds a line from the Greek tragedians that the field of iniquity produces the fruit of death. Henry adds that those who plough plough in hope, and that these are paid in their own coin. But Henry hears worse in the figure: in tracing the destruction to a blast and a breath, Eliphaz may be pointing at the wind that blew the house down on Job's children, as though they were sinners above all men.

The lions of the next two verses are read three ways, and Gill lays the options out. One Jewish commentator took the roaring lion for God himself, who tears the wicked in his wrath; two others took it for actual beasts of prey, one of the sore judgments God threatens; but Gill prefers, with two more, that oppressive rulers are meant, and in this the other voices agree with him. Henry takes the destruction apart in four stages: they shall not terrify, their roaring being stopped; they shall not tear, the teeth of the young lions being broken; they shall not enrich themselves, the old lion being famished for lack of prey; and they shall not leave a succession, the whelps being scattered to forage for themselves.

That five different words for lion stand in these verses is noticed by three voices, who draw different conclusions. Clarke lists their derivations, from tearing off, from the black lion said to be found in Ethiopia and India, from the young lion that hides to surprise its prey, from trampling, and from the lioness giving suck, when she is peculiarly fierce; then he deflates his own list, since in time such words serve only to name the beast, much as we say the lion, the king of beasts and the monarch of the forest without meaning anything by each. Ellicott draws the opposite kind of inference from the same fact, that so many words show these animals to have been common and of various kinds in Job's country. Wesley and Henry both end by suspecting that Job is the lion intended, the greatest of the men of the east, as though his estate had been got by spoil; and if that is the drift, Henry says, it was a pity that a man whom God praised should be so abused.
12:
Eliphaz now leaves reason and experience for a revelation, and the first question is whether it is to be credited. Gill reports that some have thought it a mere fiction of Eliphaz, and some have gone so far as to pronounce it diabolical, and answers them on three grounds: nothing in its manner or matter disagrees with a divine vision; Eliphaz, mistaken as he was, was a good man, as the sacrifice afterwards accepted for him shows; and Job never charges him with falsehood here. Clarke grants the vision and suspects the use made of it, since Eliphaz professes it to give himself the more authority, and applied it otherwise than the communication itself designed. Henry's verdict is the same but exacter: it would have been well had he kept to the purport of the vision, which grounds a reproof of Job's murmuring but not a charge of hypocrisy.

How the word came is dwelt on by all of them. It was brought by stealth, literally stolen for him, Ellicott notes, the word Joseph uses of himself; Wesley compares the still small voice in which God's word came to the prophets. Only a little was received, and Ellicott adds that the word for little occurs only once more, in Job's own mouth, and means little against the inexhaustible store left unrevealed; Henry makes the point generally, that it is but a little of divine knowledge the best receive here, and credits Eliphaz with not pretending to have understood the whole. Wesley distinguishes dreams, given to men asleep, from visions, given to men awake, and observes that Eliphaz was not asleep. Terror came first: Gill lists the precedents, Abraham in the vision of the pieces, Moses on the mountain, Daniel, and traces the trembling to a consciousness of guilt before the majesty of God; Henry turns it into a principle, that whom God intends to honour he first humbles and lays low.

What passed before his face is read four ways. Henry holds the apparition real and not a fancy, since an image stood plainly before his eyes, and will not allow that false visions and credulous men disprove apparitions altogether. Wesley agrees that it was an angel in visible shape, since otherwise it could not have been discerned at all. Gill reports that some take the word for a wind blowing in his face, the Targum making it a stormy wind of the kind Elijah perceived, but prefers with Jarchi an angel in human form, passing and repassing so as to be noticed. Ellicott rejects the whole way of putting the question. It is vain, he says, to argue from this passage that spiritual essences can be seen by the bodily eye, since a manifestation to the spirit can be made only to the spirit, and seeing a spirit would mean seeing the invisible; what is conceivable is that the inner perceptions may be so vivid as to take on the character of outward manifestations.

Three voices treat the passage as literature. Clarke quotes a writer who holds it vain to search ancient or modern poetry for a rival description, and who lists its powers: the midnight solitude, the deep sleep of all around, the hair erect over the whole body, the shivering not of the muscles only but of the bones, the gliding approach of the spectre, the abruptness of its pause, its indescribable form. Ellicott observes only that the language is highly poetical and has been versified in one of Byron's Hebrew Melodies. Henry accounts for the one thing a reader might complain of, that the form could not be discerned, by saying the man's conscience was to be awakened and informed, not his curiosity gratified; and on the silence before the voice he holds that when we are to speak either from God or to him it becomes us to do it with a solemn pause.
17:
The message itself is a question, and the voices disagree about what it asks of us. Ellicott calls it the burden on which Job's friends are for ever harping, perfectly orthodox and perfectly inadequate to the case, since Job will readily admit that no man can be just with God, and his dilemma then arises undiminished: where is God's justice if he punishes the innocent as the guilty? Gill objects to the comparative sense on another ground: that no man is more righteous than God is clear from reason, and an angelic spirit would hardly be sent in so awful a manner to declare it. Clarke renders it as asking whether weak and sinful man can be justified before God, and protests that it is false to infer from the words of this spectre that no man can be justified, when God justifies the ungodly; the meaning can be no more than that no man can make atonement for his own sins. His parenthesis is the sharpest thing in the chapter: whether the apparition came from heaven or hell we do not know, since its communication rankles a wound without providing a cure. Henry, taking the question as a reproof of murmuring rather than proof of hypocrisy, asks only whether the clay shall contend with the potter.

On the angels in whom God puts no trust, the dispute is over a tense. Clarke insists the verb is charged and not chargeth, so that the folly was imputed to the angels who kept not their first estate and is not laid to those who stand; Wesley agrees that the fallen are meant. Ellicott holds the opposite, that the statement is general and refers to no past act, and that we should read putteth and chargeth. Clarke also shows how unsettled the second clause is, the versions giving variously that God found perverseness in his angels, that he puts light into them, and that he put amazement in them; the Hebrew word, he notes, comes from a root meaning to irradiate. Henry offers a sense of his own, got by repeating the negation: God will put no trust in his saints nor glory in his angels, since it is his glory that he is infinitely happy without them.

The houses of clay bring the argument down to men, and here the received English is questioned. Clarke prefers the Latin's how much more to the familiar how much less: if angels may be unstable, how can man claim stability who dwells in an earthen tabernacle and must return to dust? Gill takes the house for the body in which the soul dwells, which shows the soul can exist without the body, as it does before the resurrection. Henry makes the body a clog and a cage to the soul, founded in dust so that its own weight will sink it. On being crushed before the moth, Clarke observes that the slightest accident often destroys, a fly or a grape-stone having killed great men.

The last two verses are read as the common, unremarked fact of dying. Clarke notes that in almost every moment some human being enters the world and some departs, and that the dead are soon forgotten, which he compares with the prophet's complaint that the righteous perishes and no man lays it to heart. Ellicott suspects the next verse implies that men are unmindful of their own decay, it being so insidious and so complete. Henry has death still working in us like a mole digging our grave at each remove, a man's birth and death being the sunrise and sunset of one day. On dying without wisdom Clarke turns the phrase on his own age, since with all our boasted arts we understand neither matter nor spirit, nor the gravitation by which the heavens are explained; we die without wisdom, and must die to learn these things.
